title: The sun's gift in the forest
hook: the Brahmanas follow the exiles into the forest, and Yudhishthira has nothing to feed them until the sun gives a vessel
carry: surya: the sun who ripens food for all
tomorrow: Where was Krishna during the game?

segments.voice: Yesterday the Pandavas walked into the forest. In Hindu teaching the forest is for growing, not only loss: vanaprastha.

A crowd is following the exiles. The Pandavas have lost their kingdom, their wealth and their palace, and still a company of Brahmanas keeps walking behind them into the trees, refusing to turn back. That night, by the water, Yudhishthira lies awake with a very practical problem. He can't send his guests away; a host doesn't do that. And he has nothing to feed them. How do you feed the people who chose to stay?
screen: `A CROWD FOLLOWS THE EXILES.` → `NOTHING TO FEED THEM.` → `HOW DO YOU FEED THOSE WHO STAY?`

segments.voice: The family priest, Dhaumya, gives him counsel. Turn to Surya, the sun, he says: it is the sun that ripens what the earth gives, and so feeds every creature. In Ganguli's telling, Dhaumya teaches him a hundred and eight names of the sun. So Yudhishthira purifies himself with water, and praises the sun. And Surya appears, blazing, with a gift: a copper vessel. Whatever is cooked in your kitchen, the sun tells him, won't run out for your guests, as long as Draupadi hasn't yet eaten. So the forest household finds its shape. Draupadi serves the Brahmanas first, then her husbands, and only after everyone has eaten does she eat, and the vessel is done for the day. Here's the teaching under the story. Hindus honor the sun as a god, Surya, because every meal starts with him: he ripens the grain. That's why so many Hindus still greet the morning sun by pouring out a little water toward it, an offering called arghya, often standing in a river. And at the autumn festival of Chhath, families from Bihar and nearby regions fast, then stand in rivers and lakes at sunset and again at sunrise, offering to the sun in thanks for harvest and life. When the Pandavas had lost everything, they started by thanking the one who feeds every creature. Their camp didn't get a palace back. It got a table.
screen: `DHAUMYA: TURN TO THE SUN.` · `A COPPER VESSEL FROM SURYA.` · `FOOD LASTS UNTIL DRAUPADI EATS.` · `ARGHYA. CHHATH.` · then, large: `THE SUN FEEDS EVERY CREATURE.`

segments.voice: Hold a glass of water, or picture one, and face the brightest window you have. Many Hindus offer water toward the morning sun, arghya, with a simple line like om suryaya namah. If you pray, say it and give thanks for the food today will bring; if you don't, pour the water on a plant tomorrow and think of the sun inside your next meal.
Vana. The forest of exile, where the Pandavas keep a table with almost nothing but a vessel from the sun.
Your line: surya: the sun who ripens food for all. In the forest, his gift fed every guest first. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The story of Surya's vessel is retold in Hindu storytelling, and the sun's place as the giver of food lives on in the daily offering of water, arghya, and in the festival of Chhath.

Surya.meaning: the sun, honored as a god

Chhath.meaning: a festival of thanks to the sun, kept standing in water at sunset and sunrise
